prompt: What did `page where.html` print, and why?
hint: The browser and Node add different things around the language.

choices.text: `object undefined`, because the browser has `process` and no `document`
choices.why: That is what Node printed, and the reason is reversed.

choices.text: `undefined object`: the page has `document` and no `process`
choices.why: Right. The browser adds the page; Node adds the computer.

choices.text: An error, because a page cannot run a separate `.js` file
choices.why: `<script src="where.js">` loads the file and runs it; that is the common way to do it.

choices.text: `undefined undefined`, since `typeof` is a Node feature
choices.why: `typeof` is part of the language, so both hosts have it.

prompt: Which part of a JavaScript program is the same in the browser and in Node.js?
hint: Look at the middle of the figure.

choices.text: The objects each host adds, such as `document` and `process`
choices.why: Those are exactly what differs between them.

choices.text: Nothing; they are two dialects that share a name
choices.why: The engine is V8 in both and the syntax is identical.

choices.text: The language itself: its syntax, its values, its functions
choices.why: Right. The hosts differ in what they add around it.

choices.text: The file-system functions, which every host provides
choices.why: A page has no access to your files; `fs` is Node's.

prompt: You want to check what `7 % 3` gives without creating a file. Which command does that?
hint: One flag evaluates and prints.

choices.text: `node 7 % 3`
choices.why: `node` takes a file name, so this looks for a file called `7`.
Right: `-p` evaluates the expression and prints the result.
`page` opens an HTML file in the browser; it does not evaluate an expression.

choices.text: `echo 7 % 3`
choices.why: `echo` prints its arguments as text, so this shows `7 % 3` and calculates nothing.

prompt: Match each way of running JavaScript at home with what the section says about it.
hint: One is recommended, one needs no files, one keeps your code elsewhere.

pairs.right: Recommended: runs files as this course does
Free, one line at a time, no files
Your code lives on someone else's server

right_distractors: Required before the browser can run any script

prompt: Right after installing Node.js, a terminal says `node: command not found`. What does the section suggest first?
hint: When does a terminal read its `PATH`?

choices.text: Reinstall Node.js with administrator rights
choices.why: Possible later, but the cheaper cause is checked first.

choices.text: Close the terminal and open a new one
choices.why: Right. A terminal reads `PATH` when it opens, so one opened before `~/.local/bin` existed never looks there.

choices.text: Rename the program file to end in `.node`
choices.why: The shell did not find `node` itself; the file name has not been read yet.

choices.text: Run the file with `page` instead of `node`
choices.why: `page` opens HTML pages, and it needs Node to run at all.

prompt: `node hello.html` stops with `SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<'`. What happened?
hint: What does `<` start?

choices.text: The page has a typo inside its `<script>` element
choices.why: The error is on line 1, before any script: Node read the whole file as JavaScript.

choices.text: Node 22 is too old for HTML5
choices.why: Node does not read HTML at any version.

choices.text: Node was given a page; a page goes to a browser
choices.why: Right. `<` is where HTML starts, and it is not a token of JavaScript.

choices.text: The file uses typographic quotes
choices.why: That gives `Invalid or unexpected token`, and points at the quote.

prompt: In `Error: Cannot find module '/home/ana/js/helo.js'`, which part tells you how to fix it?
hint: Node reports what it tried.

choices.text: The full path Node tried, which shows the misspelt name
choices.why: Right: the file is `hello.js`, and the path also shows which directory Node looked in.

choices.text: The indented lines under it, which list where in your file it failed
choices.why: Those are Node's own internals; your file never ran.

choices.text: The word `Error`, which means Node needs reinstalling
choices.why: Node ran fine; it simply found no such file.

choices.text: `Node.js v22.22.0` at the bottom, which shows the version is wrong
choices.why: Node prints its version after every crash; 22 is what this course uses.

prompt: Put the checks in the order the section's advice implies, for a program that will not run on a new machine.
hint: Start with whether there is a Node at all.
items: Check you are in the file's directory with `pwd` and `ls`
Run the file and read the line naming the file and line number
Open that line and fix the token it points at
trap: Editing the program first wastes time when the real cause is that Node is missing or the terminal is elsewhere.

prompt: Why did `book()` return `undefined` in `asi-return.js`?
hint: Where did the `return` statement end?

choices.text: The object has no semicolon after its closing brace
choices.why: It does have one, and a missing one would not change this.

choices.text: `title` is not a valid property name
choices.why: It is valid; the object was never reached.

choices.text: A line break straight after `return` ended the statement
choices.why: Right. The function returned nothing, and the object below was never evaluated.

choices.text: `console.log` prints objects as `undefined`
choices.why: It printed the value it was given, which was `undefined`.

prompt: In `asi-join.js`, the error says `shelf is not a function` on line 2. Why line 2?
hint: A line that starts with `(` can continue the one above.

choices.text: The parenthesis on line 3 is a typo for a brace
choices.why: The parenthesis is what ana meant; the missing semicolon is the issue.

choices.text: Lines 2 and 3 were read as one call: `shelf(function () {…})`
choices.why: Right. No semicolon was inserted, so the string was called.

choices.text: `const` cannot hold a string
choices.why: It can hold any value.

choices.text: Node counts lines from zero
choices.why: Node counts from one; line 2 is `const label = shelf`.

prompt: In a codebase written without semicolons, a line starting with which of these needs a `;` in front of it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three characters can continue the line above.

choices.why: Yes: it can be read as a call of whatever ended the line above.
Yes: it can be read as indexing the line above.

choices.text: `const`
choices.why: A keyword cannot continue an expression, so the break ends the statement.

choices.text: a backtick
choices.why: Yes: it can be read as a tagged template of the line above.

prompt: The rule that fills in a missing `;` where a line break completes a statement is called automatic semicolon ___.
hint: One word: what the engine does with the semicolon.

prompt: `const shelf = ["Dom Casmurro"]; shelf.push("Iracema");` What happens?
hint: Is `push` a reassignment?

choices.text: `TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.`
choices.why: That comes from `shelf = …`, which points the name elsewhere. `push` does not.

choices.text: The array grows to two titles
choices.why: Right. `const` fixes the name, and the array it names can still change.

choices.text: A copy of the array grows and `shelf` keeps one title
choices.why: `push` changes the array in place; there is no copy.

choices.text: A `SyntaxError`, because arrays need `let`
choices.why: Any value can be declared with `const`.

prompt: `block.js` printed `nineteenth` and then stopped. What stopped it?
hint: Where was `century` declared?

choices.text: `century` was declared with `let`, so it can only be read once
choices.why: A `let` name can be read as often as you like inside its block.

choices.text: A `TypeError`, because `century` was reassigned
choices.why: Nothing reassigned it, and the error was a `ReferenceError`.

choices.text: A `ReferenceError`: outside the `if` block, `century` was never declared
choices.why: Right. Outside the braces it was never declared.

choices.text: The `if` was false, so nothing after it ran
choices.why: 1899 is less than 1900, and `nineteenth` printed.

prompt: A function adds up prices in a loop into a name called `total`. How should `total` be declared, by the section's rule?
hint: Will `total` be given a new value?

choices.text: With `const`, because every name should be `const`
choices.why: `const` is the default, and `total` is reassigned on every turn, which `const` refuses.

choices.text: With `var`, because it is a counter
choices.why: The section finds no case where `var` is the better choice in new code.

choices.text: With `let`, since it is reassigned as the loop runs
choices.why: Right: `const` by default, `let` when the name will be pointed at a new value.

choices.text: It need not be declared, since it is inside a function
choices.why: A name is declared before use; lesson 20 shows what an undeclared one does.

prompt: Changing what is inside an array or an object, without pointing the name elsewhere, is called ___.
hint: Lesson 4 is about it.

prompt: What does `const wrong = (title) => { title: title };` return when called?
hint: After `=>`, what does a brace open?

choices.text: `{ title: 'Iracema' }`, the object
choices.why: That is what `right` returns, with parentheses.

choices.text: `undefined`
choices.why: Right. The braces are a function body with a label inside, and nothing is returned.

choices.text: A `SyntaxError` at the colon
choices.why: `title:` is a label, which is legal syntax.

choices.text: The string `"Iracema"`
choices.why: A label does not return its expression.

prompt: Which arrow returns the object `{ year: 1899 }`?
hint: Something has to stop the brace being a block.

choices.why: The braces open a block here.

choices.text: `() => return { year: 1899 }`
choices.why: `return` needs braces around the body; this is a `SyntaxError`.
Right: the parentheses make the braces an expression.
Square brackets make an array, and `year:` is not allowed inside one.

prompt: `describe("Iracema")` printed `Iracema (unknown), ? years old`. Where did `unknown` come from?
hint: Look at the parameter list.

choices.text: The default in `year = "unknown"`, used when no year is passed
choices.why: Right. A missing argument takes the default.

choices.text: JavaScript prints `unknown` for every missing value
choices.why: A missing value is `undefined`; `unknown` was written by ana.

choices.text: The `typeof` check, which returns `"unknown"` for strings
choices.why: `typeof` returns `"string"` for a string; the `?` came from that check.

choices.text: The arrow function's implicit return
choices.why: This arrow has braces, so its return is explicit.

prompt: `shelf.js` printed four numbers on its first line, for `double`, `triple`, `half` and `square` of 4. What is the sum of the four?
What is the difference between `'…' + year + '…'` and `` `…${year}…` `` in `template.js`?
hint: Compare the two lines of output.

choices.text: The template turns `year` into text and `+` keeps it a number
choices.why: Both end up as text inside a string.

choices.text: The template is faster
choices.why: The section claims nothing about speed.

choices.text: Nothing in the output; the template is easier to read
choices.why: Right. The printed lines are identical.

choices.text: `+` adds 1899 to the text as arithmetic
choices.why: With a string on one side, `+` joins; lesson 2 has the rule.

prompt: Why did `` console.log(`C:\notes\today`) `` print the path in pieces?
hint: What are `\n` and `\t` inside a string?

choices.text: Templates cannot contain a colon
choices.why: The `C:` printed fine.

choices.text: Backslashes are not allowed in templates
choices.why: They are allowed, and they start escape sequences.

choices.text: `console.log` wraps long lines
choices.why: It does not; the break came from the string itself.

choices.text: `\n` became a line break and `\t` a tab
choices.why: Right. `String.raw` keeps them as typed.

prompt:
A page builds `` `

${comment}

` `` from what a visitor typed. What does the section say a template does about HTML inside `comment`?
hint: A template joins strings.

choices.text: It escapes it, which is why templates replaced `+`
choices.why: Templates replaced `+` for readability; they escape nothing.

choices.text: It refuses to run if the value contains `<`
choices.why: Any text is accepted.

choices.text: Nothing: the HTML stays HTML
choices.why: Right. Lesson 11 shows the safe way to put text into a page.

choices.text: It strips the tags and keeps the text
choices.why: A template does not look at what it joins.

prompt: Match each piece of `tagged.js` with what it received or printed.
hint: A tag gets the fixed pieces and the values separately.

prompt: Which of these lines throws when it runs?
hint: Two of them change what is inside something; one points a name elsewhere.

choices.text: `const list = []; list.push(1);`
choices.why: A mutation; the name still points at the same array.

choices.text: `let n = 1; n = n + 1;`
choices.why: `let` may be reassigned.

choices.text: `const n = 1; n = n + 1;`
choices.why: Right: `TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.`

choices.text: `const o = { a: 1 }; o.a = 2;`
choices.why: Changing a property is a mutation, not a reassignment.

prompt: ana writes `const area = (w, h) => { w * h };` and gets `undefined`. Which fix keeps it an arrow and returns the product?
hint: Braces after `=>` make a block.

choices.text: `const area = (w, h) => ({ w * h });`
choices.why: Parentheses make the braces an object literal, and `w * h` is not a valid property.

choices.text: `const area = (w, h) => w * h;`
choices.why: Right: without braces the expression is returned. `{ return w * h; }` works too.

choices.text: `const area = w, h => w * h;`
choices.why: Two parameters need parentheses; this declares `area = w` and a stray arrow.

choices.text: `const area => (w, h) { w * h };`
choices.why: This is not valid syntax.
